blocks.q: AuthN vs AuthZ vs JWT vs OAuth vs OIDC?
a_bullets: ==Authentication== = __who is this?__ (identity proof)
==Authorization== = __what may they do?__ (permission)
{blue:JWT} = a token **format** — signed, self-describing
{blue:OAuth 2.0} = an authorization **framework** — how tokens are issued
{blue:OIDC} = authentication layered on top of OAuth

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: OAuth was **never** an authentication protocol. `scope=openid` is the bolt-on that makes login honest.

blocks.q: Why is it called a bearer token (RFC 6750)?
a_bullets: Whoever ==bears== it can use it — like cash
**No** proof-of-possession: no key, no signature from you
Steal the string, you **are** the user
So: `HTTPS` only, and ==short lifetimes== (5-15 min)
Damage window = remaining `exp`, nothing else

blocks.text: Contrast: a {purple:sender-constrained} token (DPoP, mTLS) makes the holder prove a key — covered on page 9.

items: Access logs store the full URL — token in plaintext forever
`Referer` header ships it to any third-party asset
Browser history + shared links carry it too

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Tokens for {green:machine-to-machine} and {green:cross-domain APIs}. One first-party web app on one domain? A plain **server session** is still the correct answer — do not add OAuth for the aesthetics.

slides.page_title: Round Trip, Session vs Bearer, Core Claims

blocks.q: What does a full round trip look like?
a_bullets: Login once at the ==authorization server==, get a token
Present it on **every** call to the ==resource server==
Resource server verifies locally, no login state kept

items: ==Stateless trade==: you skip a DB read, you buy ==stale authorization== until `exp`
Fire a user at 10:00, a 15-min JWT still works at 10:14
Opaque = random string, meaningless to client, validated by __introspection__ (page 10)

blocks.title: NumericDate = SECONDS
blocks.text: `exp`/`nbf`/`iat` count ==seconds since epoch==, never milliseconds. Ship `Date.now()` raw and your **1000x** token stays valid ~50,000 years.

spec.caption: Sign what was sent, not what you re-serialised

slides.subtitle: Vocabulary and trade-offs

rows: the way a token is obtained
the acting identity at the API

blocks.q: What exactly are those three dot-separated blobs?
a_bullets: Three ==base64url== segments: `header` **.** `payload` **.** `signature`
Signing input = __first two segments plus the dot__, byte-for-byte as sent
Re-encoding to "clean it up" __breaks__ the signature
base64url is {red:encoding, not encryption} — anyone can read payload
So: no secrets, no PII, no passwords, no card numbers inside

blocks.q: Which fields are standard, and what is each checked against?
a_bullets: Header: `alg` signing algorithm, `typ` = `JWT` or `at+jwt`, `kid` key id
`kid` picks the key from JWKS — see __page 3__
`iss` vs expected issuer string; `aud` vs this API's id
`sub` = the user/subject; `jti` = unique token id for replay lists

items: `jwt.decode()` reads bytes and **checks nothing** — no key touched
Trusting a decoded `role:admin` is an ==auth bypass==, not a bug
Attacker edits payload, re-encodes, leaves signature garbage — decode still succeeds
Putting a password or an internal id in the payload = publishing it

blocks.title: Page 2 in one line
blocks.text: Three base64url parts, ==public payload==, seconds-not-millis dates, compact JWS — and a decode that skips the key proves **nothing**. Verification order: __page 4__.

slides.page_title: Decoding a Real Token: JWS vs JWE

blocks.q: What falls out when I split a real token on the dots?
a_bullets: Segment 1 decodes to header JSON, segment 2 to payload JSON
Segment 3 is ==raw signature bytes==, not text — base64url of binary
`scope` is one {blue:space-delimited string}, not an array
Claim bloat is real: proxies cap headers near ==8KB== — nginx default 8k

blocks.q: Is a JWT signed or encrypted, and why always three parts?
a_bullets: ==JWS== = signed, payload readable — this is **99%** of tokens in the wild
==JWE== = encrypted, payload hidden, {purple:five} segments not three
"A JWT" in the wild means {green:JWS Compact Serialization}
JSON serialization holds multiple signatures + unprotected headers
Compact form has no whitespace and is URL-safe, so it fits a header

blocks.note: decode and verify are separate calls

blocks.q: Q: What does the signature actually prove?
a_bullets: Signature covers ==header.payload== bytes as sent
Proves __issuer minted it__ and nothing was edited
Two worlds: {red:symmetric} (one shared secret) vs {green:asymmetric} (key pair)

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Ask **who verifies**. One service you own = HS256 ok. Anyone else verifies = asymmetric, always.

items: ==ES256/EdDSA sigs ~64 bytes== vs RS256 ~256 — 4x smaller header
EdDSA/Ed25519: fast, no curve-parameter footguns
HMAC secret needs __≥256 bits of real entropy__

slides.subtitle: Header. Payload. Signature

blocks.q: Q: Why can't I just use HS256 everywhere?
a_bullets: **HS256/384/512**: same secret signs AND verifies
So {red:every verifier can forge tokens} — fine only inside one trusted service
**RS256/PS256/ES256**: private key signs at issuer, public key verifies anywhere
Third-party verifiers get the __public__ key only — they can never mint

blocks.title: Key rotation order
items: 1. Publish new key in JWKS ({green:before} signing)
2. Wait one cache TTL, then sign with new `kid`
3. Keep old key until __longest-lived token expires__
Drop the old key too early = mass 401 storm

blocks.note: pin alg server-side, never from header

blocks.title: Rule
blocks.text: Algorithms are a **server-side allowlist**. The token never gets a vote.

slides.page_title: JWKS Discovery and the Verify Order

blocks.q: Q: How does an API get the public key?
a_bullets: Discovery: `GET /.well-known/openid-configuration` gives `jwks_uri`
Keys live at `/.well-known/jwks.json` — array of JWKs, each with a ==kid==
Read `kid` from the token header, pick the matching JWK
{blue:Cache JWKS with a TTL} (~1h); refetch once on an unknown `kid`
Verify signature **first**, then check `iss`/`aud`/`exp`

items: Trusting the token's own `alg` header to pick the verifier
`alg: none` accepted — empty signature, anyone is admin
**RS256→HS256**: attacker signs HMAC using your ==public key== as the secret; a naive verifier accepts it
Dictionary HMAC secret (`secret`, `changeme`) — cracked offline from __one captured token__
One JWKS fetch per request — self-DoS on the issuer

blocks.q: In what order must a token be validated?
a_bullets: parse segments → **pin** `alg` server-side → resolve key by `kid`
verify ==signature== first — an unsigned payload is attacker text
then claims: `iss` → `aud` → `exp`/`nbf` → `scope`/`roles`
last: optional `jti` __replay__ check against a short-lived store

slides.subtitle: HS256, RS256, ES256, JWKS

blocks.q: What counts as a matching issuer and audience?
a_bullets: `iss` must **equal** the expected string — `==`, never `contains`
`https://auth.acme.com/` ≠ `https://auth.acme.com` (trailing slash)
`aud` must contain __this API's__ identifier, not just any value
One issuer mints for many APIs; `aud` is what keeps them apart

blocks.q: How much slack on exp and nbf?
a_bullets: Allow ==30–60s== leeway both directions, never unbounded
Leeway is a bandage; run __NTP__ on every verifier
5-minute leeway on a 5-minute token = double the lifetime
`nbf` in the future by more than leeway → reject, don't sleep

blocks.note: algorithms from config, never from header

items: 401 = ==re-authenticate==; the client should refresh and retry
403 = don't retry, the token is fine and still won't work
Sending 403 for an expired token stops refresh loops from working

blocks.note: ownership lives at the data layer

slides.page_title: 401 vs 403, Bypasses, and OAuth's Two Channels

items: Signature verified, `aud` skipped — a **low-trust** service's token opens a high-trust API
`except Exception: user = anonymous` — failure falls through to an allowed path
Treating `sub` as an email or display name; `sub` is __opaque__ and issuer-scoped
Two issuers can both emit `sub="1234"` — key on `(iss, sub)`, never `sub` alone
Stopping at 'token valid' — that proves **identity**, not that they own row #42

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.text: A verified signature only says the issuer wrote this. `iss` + `aud` say it was written **for you**; `exp` says it is still current; `scope` says what it may do — and ownership checks at the data layer say which rows. Skip any one and the rest is decoration.
OAuth 2.0 = ==delegated access== without sharing the password. The **valet key** model: hand a key that starts the car but won't open the trunk.

a_bullets: Front = ==via the browser URL==; user and any extension can read it
**Never** put a client secret or token in the front channel
Back = direct server→server POST over __TLS__, no browser hop
Code arrives front, is redeemed back — that split is the design

slides.subtitle: The full checklist

a_bullets: {blue:Resource owner} — the human who owns the data
{blue:Client} — the app asking on their behalf
{blue:Authorization server} — authenticates, issues tokens
{blue:Resource server} — the API that checks the token

blocks.title: Shipped code is not a secret
blocks.text: A secret in a SPA bundle or an APK is public the moment you release it. Public clients authenticate with ==PKCE==, not a secret (page 6).

items: `redirect_uri` — __pre-registered__, matched **exactly**: no wildcards, no prefix match
`state` — random, checked on return: stops **CSRF** / login fixation
`nonce` — OIDC only, echoed into the `id_token`: binds it to this request
Scopes are coarse asks; AS may grant ==fewer== than requested (downscoping)

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.text: Four roles, two channels. Front channel carries a **code** and `state`; back channel carries the **secret** and the tokens. Exact `redirect_uri`, scopes ≠ permissions.

slides.page_title: Auth Code + PKCE: The Flow to Use

items: Treating ==scopes as roles== — scope limits the **client**, not the user
`scope=admin` on a token ≠ the user is an admin; RS must still check policy
Prefix-matching `redirect_uri` — `https://app.com.evil.io` matches, code stolen
Skipping `state`, or reusing a fixed value: no CSRF protection at all
Client secret in a SPA, or tokens in the `/authorize` redirect

a_bullets: Code flow: browser gets a __one-time `code`__, backend swaps it for tokens
==PKCE== (RFC 7636) binds that code to the client that started the dance
Tokens never touch the front channel — only the short `code` does
{green:The only user-facing grant worth using in 2026}

items: Client makes `code_verifier`, derives `code_challenge`
Redirect to `/authorize` with challenge + `state`
User authenticates and **consents** at the AS
AS redirects back with `code` + `state` (front channel)
Client POSTs `code` + `code_verifier` to `/token` (back)
AS returns access + refresh (+ `id_token`)

slides.subtitle: OAuth 2.1 default

caption.text: Your login works until someone hands it a token you never actually verified. This carousel walks the whole bearer-token stack by hand — JWT anatomy, HS256 vs RS256 vs ES256 and JWKS, the full verification checklist, Authorization Code + PKCE, refresh rotation with reuse detection, revocation in a stateless world, and where the token should actually live in a browser. Ends with a mistake museum of real auth bypasses and a reference architecture you can copy.
